findings.summary: os.Chmod runs on filepath.Dir(dst) unconditionally, even without a perm argument, so it can change the mode of the working directory or a shared existing directory and may fail with EPERM on directories the process doesn't own.

judge.reason: Identifies unconditional os.Chmod on existing directory causing EPERM or permission changes, same as b1.

votes.label: hit
votes.reason: It describes the unconditional chmod on an existing directory, which changes its mode or fails with EPERM. This is exactly b1.

findings.label: hit

findings.summary: The perm argument is applied to the directory rather than the file, undocumented, so a caller passing 0o644 gets a directory without an execute bit and writing the file fails with permission denied.

judge.reason: Perm is intended as directory mode per the change; the claim about file permission misuse isn't the answer-key defect and is speculative about caller misuse.

votes.label: false_alarm
votes.reason: Perm is intended as directory mode per the change; the claim about file permission misuse isn't the answer-key defect and is speculative about caller misuse.

votes.label: valid_other
votes.reason: Perm applied to directory not file is a real design/doc problem, though distinct from the chmod-on-existing-dir bug.

votes.label: false_alarm
votes.reason: Complaint is about perm semantics/documentation and caller passing file mode; not the chmod-on-existing-directory defect, and speculative.

votes.label: valid_other
votes.reason: This is a different complaint from b1: the perm value goes to the directory, not the file. A file-style mode like 0o644 leaves the directory without an execute bit, so writing the file fails.

judge.reason: Test using filepath.Dir of a bare name yields '.', chmodding the package dir is a real test defect.
